INTERESTS OF AMICI CURIAE 1
Amici ar e  c urr e n t  an d  f o rm e r  l o cal  o ffi c ial s  wi th
the front-line responsibility for administering elections.
Some amici were elected to office as Republicans, some
were elected as Democrats, and some were elected in
nonpartisan races; other amici were appointed or selected
by Republicans, Democrats, or bodies with membership
from both parties. Some served in a statewide capacity
in addition to their time in local office. Collectively, amici
have 262 years of experience administering elections,
in addition to many decades of expertise advising and
consulting on election matters. They also have many
decades of service in leadership positions of local, state,
and national election-related commissions, boards, and
professional associations—including the U.S. Department
of Homeland Security’s Election Security Task Force;
the U.S. Election Assistance Commission’s Board of
Advisors, Voting Systems Standards Board, and Technical
Guidelines Development Committee; the National
Association of County Recorders, Election Officials
and Clerks; the National Association of Counties; the
Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions; the National
Association of Secretaries of State; the Republican
Association of Secretaries of State; and the Committee
for Safe and Secure Elections. Amici have implemented
state and federal election laws in 32 local jurisdictions
that today represent nearly 17 million voting-age citizens
spread across 14 different states, including some of the
1.  No counsel for a party authored this Brief in whole or in part,
and no party or counsel for a party made a monetary contribution
intended to fund the preparation of or submission of this Brief. No
one other than the amici curiae  or their counsel made a monetary
contribution to the preparation or submission of this Brief.

2
most populous counties in the country and some that are
significantly smaller. Some amici have been supervising
elections since well before the National Voter Registration
Act of 1993, 52 U.S.C. §§ 20501–20511 (“NVRA”), was
passed and have remained engaged with the election
process throughout the entire lifespan of the NVRA.
As current and former election officials closest to the
voting public, amici have special insight into the issues
raised by this case. Amici  have a strong interest in
preserving and defending the integrity of the  electoral
process that  lies at the core of our democratic
system of government, including the maintenance of
voter registries that accurately include Americans who
are eligible to vote and that accurately exclude those who
are not.
Amici take no position herein on the advisability
or legality of the particular Arizona list maintenance
program or the documentary proof of citizenship
requirement that generated the instant dispute. Rather,
amici provide insight on two points.
First, the plain text of the NVRA prohibits any
program the purpose of which is to systematically remove
ineligible voters during the 90 days before Election Day.
Contrary to the position of Petitioners and Respondents
supporting Petitioners (collectively “Petitioners”), the
90-d a y  m o r a to ri um  c o n tain s  n o  e x c e p ti o n  f o r  r e m o v al s
based on alleged noncitizenship. Amici ’s decades of
firsthand experience show why adhering to Congress’s
plain text ensures the effective election administration
that American citizens deserve.

3
Second, amici refute the argument that state voter
registration forms serve no legitimate purpose if those
forms do not require information beyond the federal
form. In amici’s experience, allowing states flexibility
to design their own forms promotes effective election
administration, even when federal and state registration
forms require the same mandatory information.
INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY OF
ARGUMENT
Petitioners urge this Court to interpret a provision of
the National Voter Registration Act in a manner at war
with its plain text, undermining its primary purpose.
Section 8(c)(2)(A) of the NVRA reads: “A State
shall complete, not later than 90 days prior to the date of a
primary or general election for Federal office, any program
the purpose of which is to systematically remove the names
of ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible voters.”
52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
Petitioners and their supporting amici ask the Court
to rewrite that text to create an exception for programs
targeting persons allegedly ineligible because they are
believed to be noncitizens. There are two problems with
this interpretation.
First, it ignores the NVRA’s plain text, which
requires the completion of “any program” aiming to
“systematically” remove the records of ineligible voters
no later than 90 days before the election. The text means
what it says. State and local officials must complete, not
later than 90 days before a federal election, any program

4
designed to systematically remove ineligible voters from
the list. There is no exception for systematic removal
programs based on alleged noncitizenship.
Second, Petitioners’ reading disregards the rationale
for the categorical text. Congress enacted a “pencils
down” period before Election Day to balance two related
interests: ensuring clean and accurate voter rolls and
protecting the due process rights of eligible voters.
Amici—current and former election officials responsible
for, inter alia, implementing the NVRA—have for decades
understood that the plain text, as written, enhances
effective election administration by preserving both
values.
Applying the plain text of the 90-day Provision does
not prevent election officials from responsibly maintaining
accurate voter rolls. Under the NVRA, officials may on the
eve of an election correct errors in individual registration
records, respond to individual voters’ requests for removal,
and remove an individual  from the registration  rolls
when their eligibility changes within the 90-day period,
or when a one-off challenge identifies a particular record
based on individualized information in a tailored process
designed for heightened accuracy. Officials also can, and
do, screen incoming registration applications during
this period, under regular procedures. And officials may
conduct large-scale, systematic removal programs at any
point in the election cycle other than the eve of the election.
As for the interest in protecting voters’ due process
rights, in amici ’s experience, a large-scale removal
of voters so close to an election invites unintentional
disenfranchisement. Even when conducted with

5
impeccable care, systematic attempts to remove
voters from the voter rolls—usually executed through
attempts to match computerized voter records to other
computerized data sources—are subject to error. The
source records may inaccurately identify eligible voters
as deceased, noncitizens, disenfranchised by convictions or
incarceration, or no longer residing in the jurisdiction. And
even when the underlying source records are accurate, the
matching process might mistakenly link an eligible voter on
the rolls to an ineligible person in the source data. Despite
election administrators’ best efforts, even the most precise
systematic list maintenance program can unintentionally
remove the names of some eligible voters. And in many
states, those erroneously removed voters could not vote a
valid ballot unless they discovered the error and secured
a correction by the applicable registration deadline.
Congress’s decision to balance these two interests
through a categorical 90-day moratorium on programs
of systematic purges promotes effective election
administration. It removes the greatest risk to eligible
voters when errors are least likely to be corrected in
advance of the election and preserves the precision of
list maintenance when that precision is most critical.
When voters are wrongfully removed from the rolls at
the eleventh hour, amici  receive the brunt of voters’
justified frustration and feel the durable impact on the
perceived legitimacy of the electoral process. Last-minute
removals also increase reliance on provisional ballots and
the post-election process, which disrupts officials’ ability
to efficiently conduct elections. The NVRA’s 90-day
period thus reflects Congress’s considered judgment that
programs of systematic removal must conclude in time
for eligible voters to address errors in that process, as a

6
safeguard for the orderly administration of elections. The
construction offered by Petitioners is neither appropriate
given the statutory text, nor necessary to give the
legislation full and meaningful effect.
Amici also respond to another argument offered by
Petitioners and their supporting amici, which similarly
misapprehends a basic tenet of effective election
administration practice. Petitioners urge this Court
to interpret the NVRA to permit states to demand
mandatory information beyond the information on the
federal voter registration form, such as documentary
proof of citizenship. In so doing, they claim that Congress’s
express authorization of the use of state-specific voter
registration forms would serve no meaningful purpose
unless those forms could require additional information.
Amici take no position on whether the NVRA permits
states to require information of applicants using state
voter registration forms beyond what is required for the
federal form. But Petitioners’ rationale for their reading
is simply incorrect. Amici’s decades of experience using
both state and federal voter registration forms highlight
that state forms have substantial value in election
administration even when they collect the same mandatory
information as the federal form.
The federal form was designed by one federal agency
as a compromise considering the needs of many different
jurisdictions. It is not ideally tailored to any one particular
state’s needs because it must be suited to all of them; it is
slow to change; and it is 27 pages long, including a cover
page and 22 pages of instructions.

7
State forms, by contrast, are tailored to local
needs even when they impose no additional mandatory
requirements. Among other functions, they may contain
features that enhance security, seek to identify applicants
who desire assistance or have special needs, streamline
processing, provide state specific guidance to applicants,
collect optional contact information for list maintenance
and voter outreach, recruit election workers, and tailor
form layout to better serve constituents. These practical
benefits mean that Congress’s authorization of state forms
facilitates efficient election administration, even when the
forms demand no additional information.
Accordingly, the Court should decline to judicially
append a new noncitizen exemption to the NVRA’s
categorical 90-day moratorium on programs of systematic
removal and reject Petitioners’ premise that state
registration forms serve no meaningful purpose unless
they require additional information.
ARGUMENT
I. THE NINTH CIRCUIT’S READING OF THE
NVRA FOLLOWS THE CLEAR STATUTORY
TEXT AS AMICI HAVE ALWAYS UNDERSTOOD
IT, WHILE ALTERNATIVES REQUIRE
REWRITING THE TEXT.
A. The plain text of the 90-day Provision supports
the uniform interpretation of the appellate
courts.
The NVRA’s “90-day Provision,” § 8(c)(2)(A) of the
statute, states in its entirety:

8
A state shall complete, not later than 90 days
prior to the date of a primary or general election
for Federal office, any program the purpose of
which is to systematically remove the names of
ineligible voters from the official lists of eligible
voters.
52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
What that means is just what it says. Section 8(c)
prohibits any program to systematically remove names
from the list in the days before a primary or general
election. That includes programs that systematically
remove individuals purported to be noncitizens.
In the opinion below, the Ninth Circuit correctly
understood the assignment: construe the statutory text
by giving the words their “ordinary, contemporary,
common meaning.” Perrin v. United States, 444 U.S. 37,
42 (1979); see also  TVA v. Hill, 437 U.S. 153, 173 (1978).
It concluded that “[a]ny program” aimed at systematic
removal of ineligible voters means “any program” aimed at
systematic removal of ineligible voters, without limitation.
Mi Familia Vota v. Fontes , 129 F . 4th 691, 715–16 (9th
Cir. 2025). This case involves records belonging to alleged
noncitizens, who are ineligible to vote under Arizona law,
Ariz. Const. art. 7, § 2(A), and are therefore ineligible
voters. A program to systematically remove the names of
noncitizens from the rolls is a program to systematically
remove the names of ineligible voters from the rolls.
Under the statute, any such program must be completed
not later than 90 days before a primary or general election
for federal office. The common meaning of the plain text
is straightforward.

9
The Ninth Circuit’s reading is consistent with the
decisions of other courts of appeals. Years earlier, the
Eleventh Circuit followed the same common-sense reading
of the plain text. Because Florida made citizenship a
requirement of voter eligibility, the Eleventh Circuit
understood that noncitizens would be “ineligible voters.”
Arcia v. Fla. Sec’y of State, 772 F .3d 1335, 1344 (11th Cir.
2014). A program to remove ineligible voters without
individualized information or investigation was a program
of “systematic” removal. Id. And the plain text of the
statute meant that “any” such program must be completed
90 days before a primary or general Federal election. Id.
The Fourth Circuit resolved the statutory
interpretation in the same way, albeit in the context of
an application for a stay rather than a decision on the
merits. Virginia Coal. for Immigrant Rights v. Beals, No.
24–2071, 2024 WL 4601052, at *1–2 (4th Cir. Oct. 27, 2024),
stayed without explanation , 2024 WL 4608863 (U.S. Oct.
30, 2024). That court objected to the attempt to exclude
noncitizens from the plain sweep of the 90-day Provision
by noting that the “argument violates basic principles of
statutory construction by focusing on a differently worded
statutory provision that is not at issue here and proposing
a strained reading of the Quiet Period Provision to avoid
rendering that other provision absurd or unconstitutional.
That is not how courts interpret statutes.” Id. at *1.
The ordinary meaning of the plain text, read in the
same manner by every appellate court to consider the
question—and by the U.S. Department of Justice, right
up until the most recent change of Administration, see
Resp. in Opp. to App. for Stay 1–2, 6, 20–28, Beals v. Va.
Coal. for Immigrant Rights , No. 24A407 (U.S. Oct. 29,

10
2024)—should be the only reason necessary to affirm the
court of appeals’ reading of the statute here.
Yet there is further Congressional evidence that
the 90-day Provision applies precisely as its plain
text indicates. For example, in the conference report
describing the effort to reconcile House and Senate
versions of the NVRA, Congress addressed a House bill
with a 90-day Provision identical in all respects to the
provision finally enacted. H.R. 2, § 8(c)(2), 103d Cong., 1st
Sess. (1993). The conferees stated, without qualification,
that the provision “does not permit a State to conduct a
systematic procedure to confirm voting lists within 90
days before a Federal election.” H.R. Rep. No. 103–66, 139
Cong. Rec. H2078–02 at H2083, 1993 WL 133442 (1993)
(Conf. Rep.). The conference committee—and, later, the
Congress—adopted this provision as is. 2 Id.
That blanket prohibition in Section 8(c)(2)(A) is readily
reconciled with the rule of construction—not a substantive
limitation of its own—that follows in Section 8(c)(2)(B).
52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(B) (“Subparagraph (A) shall not
be construed  to  p r e c l u d e ”  c e rtain  ac ti o n ” )  ( e m p h as is
added). Section 8(c)(2)(A) prohibits all programs from
systematically removing names from the official rolls
within the 90 days before an election, whatever the basis
for the program  of systematic removal. Section 8(c)
(2)(B) reminds officials that the time-limited moratorium
on systematic removal programs does not preclude their
ability to correct individual records based on individualized
2.  The conference adopted two unrelated changes to other
p ro vis i o ns  in  th e  Secti o n,  pe rtainin g  to  th e  l oca ti o ns  a t  w hi c h
voters might vote after moving, and not relevant to this case.

11
information, including the specific examples enumerated
in the Subparagraph.
Some of the specific examples in Subparagraph
B involve correspondence with individual voters: for
example, removal “at the request of a registrant.” Id.
§ 20507(a)(3)(A) (incorporated by reference in § 20507(c)
(2)(B)(i)). Some imply individualized recognition of
individualized mistakes: for example, “correction of
registration records.” Id. § 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii). And some
imply recognition that individual circumstances may
change, rendering particular individuals newly ineligible
within the 90-day window, and available for individualized
removal from the rolls: for example, by reason of “criminal
conviction” or “death.” Id. § 20507(a)(3)(B), (a)(4)(A) (both
incorporated by reference in § 20507(c)(2)(B)(ii)). State
provisions for one individual to challenge the registration
status of another individual at the polls based on reliable,
individualized information about their ineligibility would
similarly fall outside of the moratorium on programs to
systematically remove names from the official lists of
eligible voters.
That is, Congress made clear that the moratorium
on systematic mass removals should not be construed
to prohibit adjustment of individualized records on the
list based on individualized information. Subparagraph
(A) focuses on the systematic—and, as described below,
potentially error-laden—nature of a last-minute program
of list maintenance at scale; Subparagraph (B) cautions
that the prohibition on systematic removals on the eve of
an election need not preclude  individualized—and,  as
described below, more reliable—correction of individual
records. Both coexist, without artificial abridgment.

12
B. Petitioners’ and other amici’s interpretations of
the NVRA would require rewriting the statute.
Various parties and amici reach beyond the 90-day
Provision, bringing in distinct Subsections of the NVRA
to offer alternative and misguided readings of the text at
issue here. But juxtaposing those constructions with the
plain text of the 90-day Provision exposes the same logical
flaw: it is implausible that Congress intended to write the
statute that these alternative constructions propose using
the words Congress actually used. Each, instead, amounts
to a rewriting of the statute.
Several parties or amici urge a distinction between
“ineligible persons” and “ineligible voters.” See, e.g. ,
Br. for Petitioner 41–46, 50; Br. for U.S. as Respondent
32–35, 37–39; Br. for the U.S. House of Representatives
22–29; Br. for Ctr. for Election Confidence et al. 18–26.
These convoluted arguments admit that Congress
intended the 90-day Provision to preclude, in the period
before an election, some systematic removals of voters
thought to be ineligible. But—pointing to portions of the
statute other than the provision at issue here—they claim
Congress intended the 90-day Provision to authorize  a
program to systematically remove droves of records the
day before the election if those records belong to people
thought to have never been eligible. That is an awkward
construction of statutory text which prohibits “any
program” to “systematically remove” names of “ineligible
voters,” without exception. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(c)(2)(A).
It puts immense weight on a construction of the word
“voters” that is never expressly defined by the statute as
Petitioners urge, and which is, in context, at war with
the ordinary interpretation of the full sentence of Section
8(c)(2)(A).

13
Some of these same parties or amici further seem to
urge that the 90-day Provision precludes only systematic
removal due to change of residence. See, e.g. , Br. for
Petitioner 48; Br. for U.S. as Respondent 36, 39–40. They
seem to arrive at the conclusion by simple subtraction:
Section 8(a)(3) appears to allow the removal of a registrant
based only on request, conviction, death, or changed
residence; 3 Section 8(c)(2)(A) prohibits programs for
systematically removing any ineligible voters within
90 days of an election; Section 8(c)(2)(B) says that the
90-day limitation should not be construed to preclude
removal based on request, conviction, or death. And so,
the superficial logic goes, the 90-day limitation must
apply only to change of residence. Yet this imputes an
implausibly convoluted drafting process to Congress:
Congress ostensibly wanted to prohibit systematic purges
3.  Several parties or amici have raised the notion that 8(a)(3),
limiting the removal of “registrants,” might be read to preclude
election officials’ efforts to remove individuals who should never have
been placed on the rolls in the first instance—including the names
of minors, noncitizens, and fictitious entries. This issue is not before
this Court, and the Court need not reach it to conclude that 8(c)
(2)(A) means what it says.
As election officials, amici have understood that 8(a)(3) of the
NVRA does not preclude their ability to remove individuals from
the rolls who were never eligible to vote. If this Court wished to
offer a construction of “registrant” in 8(a)(3) consistent with that
understanding, such a construction would not be unwelcome. That
issue, though, seems irrelevant to construing the 90-day Provision
in 8(c)(2)(A). The 90-day Provision prohibits any program designed
to systematically remove the names of “ineligible voters,” a category
both distinct from and broader than those ineligible “registrants”
who may be subject to removal under 8(a)(3). And amici have always
understood their authority to remove individuals from the rolls who
were never eligible to be cabined by the prohibition on any program
of systematic  removal within 90 days of a federal election.

14
based on change of residence, and it did so by issuing
a blanket prohibition (8(c)(2)(A)), followed by a rule of
construction containing substantive exceptions in a crossreference swallowing the vast majority of the blanket
prohibition (8(c)(2)(B)), and then drafted a subsequent
provision devoted entirely to changes of residence
without mentioning the ostensibly specific prohibition on
systematic removals for changes of residence (8(d)). That
is, this reading asks this Court to find that when Congress
wrote “any program” of systematic removal, it meant only
removal related to change of residence — despite the
fact that the very next sentence in the very next Section
shows that when Congress intends to target removal
programs “on the ground that the registrant has changed
residence,” it explicitly says so. 52 U.S.C. § 20507(d)(1).
The contortions conflict with the clear text of the statute.
“Any program” means what it says.
In addition to conflicting with the clear text, the
alternative readings of the 90-day Provision also make
no sense. They offer no coherent rationale why Congress
might have imposed a 90-day ban on systematically
removing individuals from the voter rolls for some grounds
while allowing systematic removals for others in that
same period. The Department of Justice comes closest in
the attempt but still misses the mark, proposing a sort of
hierarchy—present in neither the text of the NVRA nor
its legislative history—in which participation by some
ineligible voters is worse than participation by others. Br.
for U.S. as Respondent at 41–42. Amici election officials
understand ineligible voters to be ineligible, period—and
understand these eligibility choices to be reserved to state
legislatures, within only constitutional limits. See Ariz.
v. Inter Tribal Council of Ariz., Inc., 570 U.S. 1, 16 (2013)

15
(“Arizona is correct that the Elections Clause empowers
Congress to regulate how federal elections are held,
but not who may vote in them.”) (emphasis in original).
Once a state legislature has lawfully determined that a
voter is ineligible to vote in a particular type of election,
neither executive officials nor courts have any mandate to
evaluate that voter’s presence or absence from the rolls
on a sliding scale.
In contrast, the provision that Congress actually
wrote—a ban on all programs designed to systematically
remove registrants in the waning days of the election
cycle—is entirely logical, and entirely consistent with
the basic structure of effective election administration.
As the bipartisan National Association of Secretaries of
State flatly told Congress in hearings leading up to the
NVRA: “Purges should never be conducted immediately
before an election.” Nat’l Ass’n Sec’y. State, Barriers
to Voting 15, reprinted in  Voter Registration: Hearing
Before the Subcomm. on Elections of the Comm. on H.
Admin., 101st Cong. 54, 73 (1989). Congress listened.
The 90-day Provision represents a careful balance of the
need to ensure clean and accurate voter rolls with the due
process rights of every eligible voter.
Unlike these alternative constructions, amici have
always understood the 90-day Provision to be consistent
with its plain text. While amici  may act to prevent
ineligible individuals from being placed on the voter rolls
at any time, remove ineligible individuals from the voter
rolls based on individualized inquiries at any time, and
systematically remove ineligible individuals from the voter
rolls during many times of the year (consistent with other
statutory and constitutional restrictions not at issue in this

16
case), amici may not execute programs within 90 days of
the election to systematically remove individuals from the
rolls who amici believe to be ineligible.
II. A FAITHFUL READING OF THE STATUTORY
TEXT FACILITATES EFFECTIVE ELECTION
ADMINISTRATION.
This faithful, plain-text reading of the NVRA
facilitates effective election administration. It prevents
in e vi ta b l e  e rr o rs  in  s y s te m a ti c  lis t  m ain te n an c e  fr o m
affecting eligible voters on the eve of an election.
Moreover, this reading of the NVRA’s plain text eases
the heavy administrative burdens on election officials that
such errors would generate, without jeopardizing effective
list maintenance.
Amici understand based on firsthand experience
that systematic removals from the voter rolls carry the
inevitable potential for error. As distinguished from
error correction based on individual correspondence or
rigorous individualized inquiry, systematic programs of
mass list maintenance attempt to match records from
election officials’ computerized voter registration lists
with names on other computerized data records. There is
nothing inherently wrong with such an effort, conducted
carefully and as a first pass for further investigation.
Indeed, Congress has directly encouraged officials to
employ computerized record matching as a tool for list
maintenance in some circumstances. See  52 U.S.C.
§ 21083(a)(2)(A)(ii) (requiring states to “coordinate”
voter registration rolls with state agency records on

17
felony status and death); but cf . id. § 21083(a)(2)(A)(i)
(specifying that any individual may be removed from the
registration rolls only in accordance with the provisions
of the NVRA). And amici have long done so—under the
proper conditions.
However, amici  have also recognized that such
mass matching is not free from error. In some instances,
the lists suggesting ineligibility are erroneous, or have
been misinterpreted. Individuals who are alive have
been thought to be dead. See, e.g. , Jake Miller, Texas
Voter Purge Marked by Mistakes, Misidentifications ,
CBS News (Nov. 14, 2012), https://www.cbsnews.
com/news/texas-voter-purge-marked-by-mistakesmisidentifications/ . Individuals who are citizens have
been thought to be noncitizens. See, e.g., Arcia, 772 F .3d
at 1341 (explaining that some individuals “were wrongly
identified as non-citizens”). Individuals who are not
disenfranchised by conviction have been thought to be
disenfranchised by conviction. See, e.g. , Sarah Rankin,
Youngkin Administration Says 3,400 Voters Removed
from Rolls in Error, but Nearly All Reinstated Now , AP
News (Oct. 27, 2023, 2:29 PM), https://apnews.com/article/
glenn-youngkin-voting-rights-virginia-c46eb357a3f64074
23a867653956e962  (stating that around 3,400 voters were
“removed from the rolls in error”). Individuals whose legal
residence remains firmly in place have been thought to
have moved, and individuals who reside at legal addresses
have been thought to be listed at improper locations. See,
e.g., N.C. State Conf. of the NAACP v. N.C. State Bd.
of Elections , No. 1:16CV1274, 2016 WL 6581284, at *6
(M.D.N.C. Nov. 4, 2016) (explaining that “thousands of [ ]
eligible voters were either in jeopardy of being purged or

18
were in fact purged from the voter rolls, placing them at
risk of being erroneously disenfranchised” close in time
to the election).
In other instances, the underlying information on the
reference list is accurate, but the matching effort goes
awry: the person on the list of ineligible individuals is not
the same individual thought to be represented on the voter
rolls. The most common such error is caused by attempts
to compare one list to another by matching individuals’
names and birthdates. Statistical science shows that
most individuals will dramatically underestimate the
prevalence of individuals with the same name and
birthdate. Given any 460 random voting-age people, there
is a 99% chance that at least two share the same full date of
birth. See Michael P . McDonald & Justin Levitt, Seeing
Double Voting: An Extension of the Birthday Problem ,
7 Election L.J. 111 (2008); see also Sharad Goel et al., One
Person, One Vote: Estimating the Prevalence of Double
Voting in U.S. Presidential Elections , 114 Am. Pol. Sci.
Rev. 456 (2020). This means that among any 460 voting-age
individuals with the same name, it is virtually guaranteed
that at least two will share the same full date of birth. In
registries of any size, this leads to many “birthdate twins.”
For example, California’s 2026 registration list contains
3480 unique entries for Maria Hernandez; Texas’s list
contains 3551 unique entries for Jose Garcia; Florida’s
list contains 1387 unique entries for James Smith; and
Pennsylvania’s list contains 1053 unique entries for Michael
Smith. From those people with those names in those
states alone, even absent the many other common first
and last name combinations, statistics predict more than
a thousand distinct individuals with the same name and
birthdate. That leaves ample opportunity for error.

19
The existence of errors in underlying information and
errors in matching means that a list maintenance program
based on comparing one large list to another is virtually
guaranteed to yield mistakes. Experience demonstrates
that this is not merely speculation: would-be purge lists
and some actual purges have indeed fallen victim to
these errors, despite the best efforts of election officials.
In 2024, for example, a federal court blocked Alabama’s
last-minute attempt to inactivate 3,251 records of alleged
noncitizens; it was later discovered that at least 2,000 (and
maybe more) of those records actually belonged to eligible
voters. Transcript at 13, Motion Hearing, Ala. Coal. for
Immigrant Justice v. Allen, No. 2:24-cv-01254 (N.D. Ala.
Oct. 16, 2024); Jude Joffe-Block, U.S. Citizens are Among
the Voters Removed in Virginia’s Controversial Purge, NPR
(Oct. 30, 2024, 11:25 EST), https://www.npr.org/2024/10/29/
nx-s1-5169204/virginia-noncitizen-voter-purge . Pressure
to engage in large-scale list management with inevitable
error is also not always self-imposed. Precisely one week
ago, with 21 days remaining in an ongoing election, the
U.S. Department of Justice demanded that Los Angeles
County refuse to tally ballots corresponding to a list of
over 20,000 voters on a “thumb drive,” delivered without
explanation of the list’s provenance or the methodology
involved in its creation, if the names on the list could not
be verified as eligible within 48  hours. Letter from
R. Trent McCotter, Acting Deputy Att’y Gen., U.S.
Dep’t of Justice, to Dean C. Logan, Los Angeles County
Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk (Oct. 13, 2026) https://
rrcc.box.com/s/jwladrl77dwd9ud2hexcw2yeuvm1gnic; see
also Complaint for Declaratory and Injunctive Relief,
United States v. California , No. 2:26-cv-12025 (C.D. Cal.
Oct. 15, 2026), ECF No. 1. Similar federal government
lists in other jurisdictions have been riddled with error.

20
Nick Corasaniti, From 16,000 to 185 to Zero: Trump’s
Claims of Illegal Voting in Nevada Fizzle , N.Y. Times
(Sept. 24, 2026), https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/
us/politics/nevada-voters-homeland-security-trump.
html?eafs_enabled=false. Election officials understand
that overly hasty, last-minute programs aiming to
systematically remove ineligible voters would inevitably,
and unnecessarily, jeopardize the rights of eligible voters
in the process.
That these errors may not be intended does not negate
their harmful effect. Amici  do not presume bad faith
when individuals or entities claim evidence of ineligible
voters on the rolls—whether that evidence comes from
private entities or government bodies. Election officials
investigate when an investigation is warranted. Amici do
their best to serve their constituents by ensuring that list
maintenance is conducted as accurately as possible, and
they presume that colleagues around the country do the
same. But as a practical matter, amici also understand
such errors to be inevitable in a program of systematic
removal, even when the removal is designed to be reliable
and conducted with the utmost care.
It is much more difficult for election officials to conduct
list maintenance with the utmost care when executed
on the eve of an election. Amici keenly understand the
existing heavy burdens on local election administrators
in the run-up to Election Day. In the final period before
an election, officials are asked to: verify petitions for
candidates and ballot measures; review, screen, and
process the increasing volume of legitimate incoming voter
registration applications and changes to existing voter
registrations; design, proofread, and print ballots; review

21
and respond to requests for absentee ballots; prepare, test,
and distribute voting systems; prepare for any early voting
process permitted in their jurisdictions; recruit and train
poll workers; prepare and distribute precinct registers;
seek and secure legally compliant polling places, and
ensure that they have sufficient equipment and resources;
respond to inquiries from candidates and the voting
public; and prepare contingency plans . . . and respond
to contingencies that no reasonable person could foresee.
Occasionally—and for some amici, quite frequently—they
must also contend with legal challenges that seek to change
the way they conduct any of the tasks above, including
serving as parties or witnesses in litigation and responding
to any modifications in procedures that the courts impose.
Adding systematic list maintenance to those tasks
decreases election officials’ ability to perform all of these
other election-related activities. Permission for belated
mass purges will also inevitably increase demands from
external groups to conduct systematic removals, including
removals based on evidence of mixed or unknown quality
which officials will have to devote time to investigating.
These burdens are cumulative and reinforce each other:
the increased load at a sensitive time further decreases
local officials’ ability to perform reliable systematic
removal with appropriate quality control. Moreover,
because amici  know that systematic list maintenance
contains inevitable errors, they have to not only perform
the mass program but also ensure adequate notice to
those affected—sometimes with multiple mailings and/or
phone calls—and accommodate the incremental responses
from eligible citizens wrongly removed. The NVRA’s 90-
day Provision provides a sensible insulation from these
unwanted and unwarranted extra burdens.

22
Purges on the eve of an election also harm voters. At
a farther remove from Election Day, eligible voters have
ample opportunity to compensate for errors that officials
are not able to eradicate from a program of systematic
list maintenance, before those voters are next asked to
vote. This process is not cost-free. Eligible voters who
have been unintentionally and mistakenly removed from
the rolls must have cause to check their registration status,
recognize the error, and either petition to correct the
error or re-register before the deadline for the upcoming
election. But at least 90 days before an election often
provides sufficient time to correct damage done by an
imperfect program.
In the final days before an election, that opportunity
evaporates. There is substantial risk that despite election
officials’ best efforts, an erroneously removed elector will
not receive timely notice of the removal. Even if notice is
timely, there may nevertheless be insufficient time for the
elector to correct the error before Election Day. If the
error generates a dispute, it may be necessary to collect
and review incremental documentation or hold a hearing,
without the benefit of time to ensure that the proceedings
are adequate for the task. This means that a last-minute
program of systematic list maintenance does not clean the
rolls: to the contrary, it makes them dirtier.
For example, a systematic program of list maintenance
executed on the night before Election Day would inevitably
remove some eligible voters from the rolls by mistake.
The likelihood of error would exist whether the program
of removal attempted to target those who are purportedly
noncitizens or those who were ineligible for any other
reason. Voters wrongfully removed would be entirely

23
dependent on post-election processes to secure their right
to vote. For those who were able to cast provisional ballots,
the process would entail post-election administrative
review or litigation, with consequent disruption rising with
the scale of the error (which itself rises with the scale of
the program of systematic removal). For those purged by
a large-scale program of systematic removal who were not
able to cast provisional ballots, there may be no remedy
at all for the loss of their fundamental right to vote.
This risk dissipates, but does not disappear, with
increasing distance from Election Day. Some eligible
citizens will attempt to vote early, in accordance with
state law. Others, by choice or by necessity, will seek to
vote by mail substantially before Election Day, to ensure
that their ballots are received in time to count. Congress
has required absentee ballots to be sent to deployed
servicemembers and civilians overseas, no fewer than 45
days before an election, and there is no reason to believe
that these voters would be immune from the errors of
programs of systematic removal. 52 U.S.C. § 20302(a)(8).
Last-minute list maintenance affects these voters far
before Election Day itself.
Moreover, last-minute systematic purges ripple
far beyond the voters removed from the rolls. Voters
erroneously removed who arrive at their polling places on
Election Day will not find themselves on the poll books, for
reasons neither they nor their poll workers are likely to
understand readily, contributing to distrust in the election
process itself. Some will attempt to phone local officials
to resolve the problem; some will vote provisional ballots.
These procedures take incremental time, disrupting
the election process for other voters and increasing the

24
length of lines and the time that every voter will stand
and wait to cast a ballot. In addition, a glut of provisional
ballots increases the time required to tabulate and report
accurate election returns; warranted or not, that postelection delay may undermine all voters’ trust in the
integrity of the system.
In these waning days of an election cycle, Congress
recognized what amici  have long understood: that
errors in a program of systematic purges might unduly
jeopardize the votes of eligible citizens and disrupt
the smooth progress of an election. The NVRA’s 90-
day “‘pencils down’” provision represents Congress’s
considered judgment as to the period of time appropriate
to ensure that the unanticipated side effects of a program
of systematic removal do not catch erroneously removed
eligible voters by surprise. It is a judgment amici heartily
support.
This judgment does not leave amici cause for concern
about the accuracy of the voter rolls. Under the NVRA
as amici have always understood it, election officials have
ample control over list maintenance. There is no federal
statutory bar to prevent tailored, effective measures to
screen applications for ineligible voters before they are
placed on the rolls. There is no federal statutory bar to
an accurate program to systematically remove ineligible
voters from the rolls at any point in the election cycle
other than the 90 days before Election Day. And there is
no federal statutory bar to an individualized correction
or removal of individual registration records, based
on individualized information beyond any systematic
removal program, at any point. The NVRA’s 90-day
Provision simply prohibits the least accurate form of list

25
maintenance precisely when it is likely to do the most
damage.
III. EVEN IF FEDERAL AND STATE REGISTRATION
FORMS REQUIRE THE SAME MANDATORY
INFORMATION, STATE FORMS’ DESIGN
FLEXIBILITY FACILITATES EFFECTIVE
ELECTION ADMINISTRATION.
As explained above, amici take no position on whether
the NVRA permits states to require information beyond
the federal form’s requirements. No matter how the
statute is construed, however, state forms do not lose
their primary purpose if they are not “more demanding”
than the federal counterpart, as Petitioner suggests. Br.
for Petitioner at 15. Amici’s extensive experience with
federal and state registration forms shows that state
control over form design offers important benefits even
when both forms require the same information. State
forms can, inter alia, contain features that enhance
security, better identify and accommodate applicants with
special needs, streamline election administration, reflect
state-specific rules and practices, expand communication
with voters, recruit election workers, and tailor the form
layout to serve constituents. A uniform federal form built
on a compromise among 50 states cannot perform locally
tailored functions as effectively. State forms therefore
allow states to “serve as a laboratory; and try novel [ ]
experiments without risk to the rest of the country.”
New State Ice Co. v. Liebmann , 285 U.S. 262, 311 (1932)
(Brandeis, J., dissenting).
First, some state forms are designed to enhance
security through tracking features. For example, in

26
Indiana, certain voter registration forms include a fivedigit NVRA tracking number that corresponds to the
government agency source of the form. This information
can be used in the event of an audit or to investigate if an
unusual number of forms from a particular source contain
errors. In contrast, the federal form does not contain such
tracking features.
Second, state forms can seek to identify applicants who
desire assistance or have special needs, more effectively
than the federal form. Utah, Nevada, and Washington,
for example, use forms that ask applicants to indicate
military or overseas status, enabling election officials to
inform these voters affirmatively about tailored voting
procedures. Hawaii’s forms ask applicants about their
relevant disability status, and the state then provides an
accessible blank electronic ballot to individuals with an
impairment that prevents them from reading standard
print. South Dakota authorizes its local officials to produce
a large-print version of the state form, for voters who find
large print easier to read. And, reflecting the needs of its
citizen population, California offers its form in languages
that the federal voter registration form does not, not only
providing voters with distinct access but also helping
officials assess the need for multilingual assistance at the
polls. Collecting this information through distinct forms
reflects legitimate state choices to help local subdivisions
serve military members, overseas voters, people with
disabilities, and citizens with limited English proficiency.
Third, state forms often include features that improve
administrative efficiency and save election officials time.
Some states allow voters to register through an online
registration portal. For example, Indiana allows applicants

27
with a verified driver’s license or state identification card
to register using its online system. Also, Utah’s form
asks whether applicants prefer to vote in person or by
mail, reducing the need for additional paperwork. This
Court has recognized the importance of elections being
“operated equitably and efficiently.” Burdick v. Takushi,
504 U.S. 428, 433 (1992).
Fourth, state voter registration forms can more
concisely reflect and educate voters about state-specific
voting laws and procedures. For example, Washington
and Massachusetts use forms that identify state-law
penalties for false information. And Utah’s form includes
information about how to request additional privacy
protections available under state law, including for victims
of domestic violence, law enforcement officers, and
members of the armed forces.  The federal form, by
contrast, cannot be tailored as closely to any one state
because it must serve all of them.
Fifth, some state forms collect optional contact
information not requested by the federal form, improving
communication with voters. Kentucky and Vermont,
for example, request applicants’ email addresses, while
Utah requests text-message information and consent.
These widely used channels enable officials to contact
voters more promptly and effectively, and the information
can be used for list maintenance. See City of Ontario,
Cal. v. Quon , 560 U.S. 746, 760 (2010) (recognizing the
“pervasive[ness]” of “text message communications”).
Sixth, states such as South Carolina and Connecticut
use registration forms to recruit election workers by
including an optional question inviting applicants to

28
express interest in serving as poll workers. Elections
require “thousands of state and local officials and
volunteers” to “participate in a massive coordinated
effort . . . during the election, and again in counting the
votes afterwards.” Democratic Nat’l Comm. v. Wis.
State Legislature, 592 U.S. 1039, 1043 (2020) (Kavanaugh,
J., concurring). This recruitment feature is especially
valuable during poll-worker shortages.
Seventh, many states have invested in tailoring
the visual design and layout of their forms in ways that
may better serve their constituents than the federal
counterpart. Occasionally, these changes reflect states’
litigation experience. For example, after several voters
did not notice particular boxes on Florida’s state
voter registration form and litigated their subsequent
disenfranchisement, Diaz v. Cobb, 541 F . Supp. 2d 1319,
1321 (S.D. Fla. 2008), Florida voluntarily revised the
visual layout of its form to make the boxes—and other
elements of the form—far more prominent.
DOJ’s NVRA guidance recognizes these various
advantages of state forms apart from the collection of
additional mandatory information. It explains that a
state “form should be easier for applicants to navigate and
easier for agencies and election officials to process.”
U.S. Dep’t of Just., Civ. Rts. Div., The National
Voter Registration Act of 1993 (NVRA): Questions and
Answers, Question 22  (Nov. 1, 2024), https://www.justice.
gov/crt/national-voter-registration-act-1993-nvra. States
can tailor their forms accordingly, whereas the Election
Assistance Commission designs the federal form through
consultation and compromise among many jurisdictions.
The guidance also notes that state forms “would not be as

29
lengthy as the federal form, which contains information
about voter registration in each state.” Id. Although
applicants complete only one page, the federal packet is 27
pages, including a cover page and 22 pages of instructions.
In contrast, many state forms are only one or two pages.
State forms therefore benefit voters and election officials
independent of any incremental required information.
CONCLUSION
Amici  take no position before this Court on the
ultimate disposition of the underlying issues in this case.
But amici  offer their experience to suggest that the
ordinary, common meaning of the plain text of the NVRA’s
90-day Provision implements a blanket moratorium on
programs to systematically remove ineligible voters from
the rolls at the precise point when such programs could
cause the most harm, and removals of alleged noncitizens
are no exception to the rule. The 90-day Provision thereby
facilitates rather than undermines effective election
administration. And amici similarly offer their experience
to relate the value for election administration in the variety
of different ways in which states design their own voter
registration forms to facilitate their own voter registration
processes, even if those state forms require the same
mandatory information as the federal counterpart.

30
Respectfully submitted,
